newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Kashmir rebel group says senior commander killed.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir rebel group says senior commander killed.

text.p: A guerrilla group India accuses of involvement in the kidnapping of four Western tourists denied on Tuesday that its leader had been killed in the Indian-ruled part of the disputed Kashmir region.

But a spokesman for the Harkat-ul-Ansar in Muzaffarabad, capital of Pakistan-ruled Azad (free) Kashmir, said another senior commander of the group had been killed in a gun-battle in Srinagar, summer capital of the Indian Kashmir, on Monday.
India's paramilitary Border Security Force (BSF) said on Monday that Harkat chief Parvez Ahmad Gazi, a Pakistani national, was killed in the with BSF personnel in Srinagar.
A Harkat spokesman earlier denied that any shootout had taken place there on Monday.
But later, the spokesman said the earlier report was found to be wrong and that the group received information later that its senior commander, whom it named Abu Gazi, was killed.
However, it said the group leader, whom it named as Peer Baba, was alive and safe.
"Indian claims of killing our chief were aimed at demoralising the freedom-fighters, but India will not succeed in its mission," the Harkat spokesman said.

Indian officials say the mysterious Al-Faran guerrilla group that kidnapped the Western tourists in July 1995 is a front for Harkat, which they say operates from the one-third of Kashmir that Pakistan rules. India controls the rest.
Harkat denies any role in the kidnappings, which it says were masterminded by Indian intelligence agencies to defame Kashmiri militants.

The tourists -- two Britons, an American and a German -- were abducted while trekking in the Himalayas. There has been no trace of the four for months. The body of a fifth hostage, a Norwegian, was found beheaded in August 1995.

Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms separatists in Kashmir, saying it provides only moral and diplomatic support to guerrillas in the region. India and Pakistan have fought two wars over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947.
Dozens of guerrilla groups seeking merger with Pakistan or independence have been fighting Indian security forces in Kashmir since 1990.
More than 20,000 people have died in violence since then.
